===== README.txt =====
stories15M — a language model that carries its own engine
=========================================================

This is a werk package: ONE FILE that carries an artifact and everything needed
to understand it. This particular one carries a language model, and "everything
needed to understand it" was taken literally.

WHAT IS IN HERE

  model/stories15M.bin       the weights. 15 191 712 parameters, f32, 58 MB.
  model/tokenizer.bin        the vocabulary. 32 000 entries.
  tools/llama2c/             the COMPLETE SOURCE of a runtime that runs it:
                             ~970 lines of C99, no dependencies, no build
                             system, no network.
  spec/layouts/              a byte-exact grammar for each of the two binary
                             formats above.
  testvectors/               what the model MUST produce, deterministically,
                             so you can tell "it ran" from "it ran correctly".
  spec/                      the werk format specification itself.
  loaders/                   three single-file, dependency-free readers for
                             this container: one Python, one Rust, one C.
  recipe/, disclosure/, provenance/, LICENSE
                             where the weights came from, what is model output
                             and what is not, and the three licences that meet
                             in this file.

HOW TO GET TEXT OUT OF IT

  1. Extract. It is a store-mode zip; any zip tool works, or use
     loaders/werk_read.py, which needs nothing but a Python interpreter.
  2. Read tools/llama2c/BUILD-AND-RUN.md. It has the exact compile command for
     each platform, says which of them were measured and on what machine, and
     says which one is upstream's and was not measured here.
  3. Build the runtime from source. There is no binary in this package.
  4. Run it. The invocation is in BUILD-AND-RUN.md §3 and in
     testvectors/vectors.json as an argv array.
  5. Check your output against testvectors/vectors.json. That step is the
     point of the package: a runtime that reads the weights at the wrong
     offsets still emits confident English, and only the vector catches it.

NOTHING HERE RUNS ITSELF

There is no compiled artifact anywhere in this package, and no werk tool
executes anything it finds in one. spec/SPEC.md §7.1 is the rule: source is
always allowed and reading it is the point; a prebuilt binary is inert data and
is never executed automatically under any circumstance, including a valid
signature. This package has no prebuilt binary at all, so every executable byte
you end up with is one you produced from source you can read.

A NOTE ON THE PROFILE

This package declares `profile: "model/1-draft"`. THAT PROFILE DOES NOT EXIST as
a ruled part of the werk specification. It was drafted while building this file,
because the file had nowhere to declare what it was, and the draft is carried
here at spec/PROFILE-MODEL-DRAFT.md together with the manifest schema it
validates against (spec/schemas/manifest.model-draft.schema.json). Section 5 of
the draft lists five places where the existing core doctrine does not fit a
model package — a missing `train` role, a hermeticity rule no model package can
satisfy, a disclosure axis that has one dimension where a model has two, a tool
role vocabulary with no word for "executor", and the absence of the node types
this package had to declare in the `x.` namespace. None of them are fixed. They
were found by building this, which is what fixtures are for.

WHAT THIS PACKAGE IS NOT

Not a benchmark: the test vectors check that execution is CORRECT, not that the
model is good. It is a 15 M-parameter story completer trained on a synthetic
children's-story corpus and it will happily contradict itself in the third
sentence.

Not a training record: the weights are the output of a run this package did not
perform and cannot reproduce. recipe/recipe.json says so, in the format's own
vocabulary, with `reproducibility: "descriptive"`.

Not fast: the carried runtime is scalar C on one core, measured at ~94 tokens
per second. Optimised executors are somebody's product and an extension-tier
concern by design; base doctrine's job is that a stranger can get output at all.

# BUILD AND RUN — the runtime this package carries

This package contains a language model and the complete source of a runtime
that executes it. This file is the exact procedure: what to compile, with what
command, and what to run to get text out. Every command below is quoted as it
was actually typed; the ones marked **VERIFIED** were run by the package's
author on the machine described in §5 and their output is what
`testvectors/vectors.json` records.

Nothing here is executed for you and nothing in this package executes itself.
`spec/SPEC.md` §7.1 is the rule and it is not softened here: source is always
allowed and reading it is the point; a compiled artifact is inert data. There is
no compiled artifact in this package — every executable byte you end up with,
you produced.

## 1. What you need out of the package

Extract the whole package (it is a store-mode zip; any zip tool, or the
zero-dependency reader in `loaders/`). Four paths matter:

| path | what it is |
|---|---|
| `tools/llama2c/run.c` | the whole runtime, ~970 lines of C99, no dependencies beyond the standard library and libm |
| `tools/llama2c/win.h`, `tools/llama2c/win.c` | a Windows shim providing `mmap`/`munmap`/`clock_gettime`. Needed on Windows ONLY; `run.c` includes `win.h` behind `#if defined _WIN32` |
| `model/stories15M.bin` | the weights, 60 816 028 bytes, f32. Layout: `spec/layouts/llama2c-checkpoint.layout.txt` |
| `model/tokenizer.bin` | the vocabulary, 433 869 bytes. Layout: `spec/layouts/llama2c-tokenizer.layout.txt` |

Toolchain: any hosted C99 compiler. Nothing is downloaded, nothing is
installed, there is no build system, no makefile is required and no network
access is needed at any point.

## 2. Build

Run these from the extracted package root.

### 2a. POSIX — Linux, macOS, WSL, MSYS2's UCRT/MSYS shells

```
cc -O3 -o run tools/llama2c/run.c -lm
```

`win.c` is NOT compiled on POSIX and MUST NOT be: `run.c` takes the
`<sys/mman.h>` branch there. This is upstream llama2.c's own build line
(`gcc -O3 -o run run.c -lm`, from its README, which this package carries at
`recipe/inputs/llama2c-README.md`). **NOT VERIFIED HERE** — the machine in §5
is Windows and had no working POSIX C compiler on it, so this command is
reported as upstream's, unmeasured, and is labelled that way rather than
claimed. If it fails for you, that is a fact worth reporting; the two commands
below are the ones that were measured.

### 2b. Windows, MSVC — **VERIFIED**

From a shell where `cl.exe` is on PATH (run `vcvars64.bat` from your Visual
Studio installation first, or use a "x64 Native Tools Command Prompt"):

```
cl /nologo /O2 /Fe:run.exe tools\llama2c\run.c tools\llama2c\win.c
```

Both `.c` files. `win.c` supplies `mmap`, `munmap` and `clock_gettime`, which
`run.c` calls and which Windows does not have. Measured: exit 0, one warning-free
`Generating Code...`, a 218 624-byte `run.exe`.

### 2c. Windows, mingw-w64 gcc — **VERIFIED TO FAIL, UNMODIFIED**

```
gcc -O3 -o run.exe tools/llama2c/run.c tools/llama2c/win.c -lm
```

does **not** build with mingw-w64 gcc 15.2.0. Measured, both errors, verbatim:

```
win.c:136: error: passing argument 4 of 'VirtualProtect' from incompatible
           pointer type   (uint32_t * vs PDWORD, i.e. unsigned long *)
win.c:175: error: redefinition of 'clock_gettime'
           (mingw's own <pthread_time.h> already defines it inline)
```

Neither is a werk problem and neither is fixed here, because fixing it would
mean shipping a `win.c` whose bytes are not the ones its author published — and
then this package's `sha256` for that file would no longer match upstream, which
is the one property that lets a stranger check where the code came from. The
two changes a consumer needs, if a mingw build is what they want, are one cast
and one `#if !defined(__MINGW32__)` guard, both inside `win.c`, both outside the
scope of this package. Use §2b instead.

Suppressing the first error with `-Wno-incompatible-pointer-types` and renaming
the second with `-Dclock_gettime=...` was also tried, and also fails: the rename
applies to mingw's own inline definition too. Recorded so nobody spends the
twenty minutes again.

## 3. Run

```
./run model/stories15M.bin -z model/tokenizer.bin -t 0.0 -n 64 -i "Once upon a time"
```

(on Windows, `run.exe model\stories15M.bin -z model\tokenizer.bin -t 0.0 -n 64 -i "Once upon a time"`)

Flags that matter:

| flag | meaning |
|---|---|
| first positional | path to the checkpoint. Required. |
| `-z <path>` | tokenizer path. **Required here**, because run.c's default is `tokenizer.bin` in the CURRENT DIRECTORY and this package puts it in `model/`. Omitting it is the single most likely way to fail. |
| `-t <float>` | temperature. **`-t 0.0` selects greedy argmax and makes the run deterministic.** Any other value samples and the output will not match the test vectors. |
| `-n <int>` | number of steps. |
| `-i <string>` | the prompt. |
| `-s <int>` | RNG seed. Irrelevant at `-t 0.0`; the sampler is never consulted. |

The generated text goes to **stdout**. A timing line (`achieved tok/s: …`) goes
to **stderr** and is not part of any test vector.

## 4. Check your result against the package

`testvectors/vectors.json` is the correctness anchor. It records, for two
temperature-0 runs, the exact command line, the exact stdout, its sha256, and
the exact sequence of token ids. Verify like this:

1. Run the command in `vectors[i].argv`.
2. Take stdout, **replace CRLF with LF**, and compare against
   `vectors[i].stdout_text` — or hash it and compare against
   `vectors[i].stdout_sha256_lf`.
3. It should match byte for byte.

The CRLF normalisation is not a fudge. `run.c` writes to a text-mode stream, so
the newlines inside the generated story come out as `\n` on POSIX and `\r\n` on
Windows from an identical model computation. The hash is therefore declared over
the LF form and the byte count of the LF form is given too
(`stdout_bytes_lf`). The raw Windows-console hash of the first vector is
recorded separately as `stdout_sha256_crlf` so that the normalisation can itself
be checked rather than taken on trust.

`vectors[i].token_ids` is the stronger anchor: token ids are integers and no
newline convention touches them. They were captured by a two-line
instrumentation of `run.c`, and that instrumentation travels in this package as
`testvectors/tokens_instrumentation.diff` so you can reproduce the capture
instead of believing it. **The unmodified `run.c` does not print token ids** —
matching `stdout_sha256_lf` is the check you can do without patching anything,
and it is sufficient.

### If it does not match

Floating-point summation order is the expected cause and it is a real one: the
runtime is scalar C, but a compiler is free to vectorise the reductions in
`rmsnorm`, `softmax` and `matmul`, and `-ffast-math` or an aggressive `-O` on a
different target will reassociate them. A greedy argmax over 32 000 logits is
usually robust to that, and it is not guaranteed to be. So:

* a run that matches **is** strong evidence the whole chain is right;
* a run that **diverges after N tokens** is evidence of arithmetic reassociation,
  not necessarily of a broken reader. Report N and your compiler flags.
* a run that produces **fluent English but a different story from token 1** means
  the prompt encoding differs — check §5 of the tokenizer layout grammar (the
  BOS token and the dummy-prefix space).
* a run that produces **garbage from token 1** means the weights are being read
  at the wrong offsets — check the dead RoPE tables in §4 of the checkpoint
  layout grammar.

## 5. The machine the vectors were produced on

Recorded because "it matched" is only a measurement if you know against what.

| | |
|---|---|
| OS | Microsoft Windows 10 Enterprise, 10.0.19045, x64 |
| CPU | AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X (32 core) |
| compiler | Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version **19.38.33143** for x64 (Visual Studio 2022 Community) |
| build command | `cl /nologo /O2 /Fe:run.exe run.c win.c` |
| binary | `run.exe`, 218 624 bytes |
| throughput | 93.75 tok/s on vector 1, 94.51 tok/s on vector 2 (from the runtime's own stderr line) |

No GPU is involved anywhere. This is a 15 M-parameter model in f32 on one CPU
core.

## 6. What this package does NOT contain

Stated so nobody looks for it:

* **no training code and no training data.** The weights are the output of a
  training run this package did not perform and cannot reproduce.
  `recipe/recipe.json` records what is known about that run — the architecture,
  the dataset by name, the publisher — with `reproducibility: "descriptive"`
  and an `unrecorded[]` list, which is the format's way of saying "this is a
  truthful record and it is not a reproduction recipe".
* **no compiled binary.** By doctrine, see the top of this file.
* **no quantised variant.** The checkpoint is f32 throughout.
* **no chat template.** `run.c` has a `-m chat` mode; the model in this package
  is a story completer trained on TinyStories and was never instruction-tuned,
  so chat mode will produce a story with the chat scaffolding wrapped around it.

typedef struct {

    float *x; // activation at current time stamp (dim,)
    float *xb; // same, but inside a residual branch (dim,)

void read_checkpoint(char* checkpoint, Config* config, TransformerWeights* weights,

    fseek(file, 0, SEEK_END); // move file pointer to end of file

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// neural net blocks; the dynamics of the Transformer

void rmsnorm(float* o, float* x, float* weight, int size) {
    // calculate sum of squares
    float ss = 0.0f;
    for (int j = 0; j < size; j++) {
        ss += x[j] * x[j];
    }
    ss /= size;
    ss += 1e-5f;
    ss = 1.0f / sqrtf(ss);
    // normalize and scale
    for (int j = 0; j < size; j++) {
        o[j] = weight[j] * (ss * x[j]);
    }
}

void softmax(float* x, int size) {
    // find max value (for numerical stability)
    float max_val = x[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (x[i] > max_val) {
            max_val = x[i];
        }
    }
    // exp and sum
    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        x[i] = expf(x[i] - max_val);
        sum += x[i];
    }
    // normalize
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        x[i] /= sum;
    }
}

void matmul(float* xout, float* x, float* w, int n, int d) {
    // W (d,n) @ x (n,) -> xout (d,)
    // by far the most amount of time is spent inside this little function
    int i;
    #pragma omp parallel for private(i)
    for (i = 0; i < d; i++) {
        float val = 0.0f;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            val += w[i * n + j] * x[j];
        }
        xout[i] = val;
    }
}

float* forward(Transformer* transformer, int token, int pos) {

    // a few convenience variables
    Config* p = &transformer->config;
    TransformerWeights* w = &transformer->weights;
    RunState* s = &transformer->state;
    float *x = s->x;
    int dim = p->dim;
    int kv_dim = (p->dim * p->n_kv_heads) / p->n_heads;
    int kv_mul = p->n_heads / p->n_kv_heads; // integer multiplier of the kv sharing in multiquery
    int hidden_dim =  p->hidden_dim;
    int head_size = dim / p->n_heads;

    // copy the token embedding into x
    float* content_row = w->token_embedding_table + token * dim;
    memcpy(x, content_row, dim*sizeof(*x));

    // forward all the layers
    for(unsigned long long l = 0; l < p->n_layers; l++) {

        // attention rmsnorm
        rmsnorm(s->xb, x, w->rms_att_weight + l*dim, dim);

        // key and value point to the kv cache
        int loff = l * p->seq_len * kv_dim; // kv cache layer offset for convenience
        s->k = s->key_cache + loff + pos * kv_dim;
        s->v = s->value_cache + loff + pos * kv_dim;

        // qkv matmuls for this position
        matmul(s->q, s->xb, w->wq + l*dim*dim, dim, dim);
        matmul(s->k, s->xb, w->wk + l*dim*kv_dim, dim, kv_dim);
        matmul(s->v, s->xb, w->wv + l*dim*kv_dim, dim, kv_dim);

        // RoPE relative positional encoding: complex-valued rotate q and k in each head
        for (int i = 0; i < dim; i+=2) {
            int head_dim = i % head_size;
            float freq = 1.0f / powf(10000.0f, head_dim / (float)head_size);
            float val = pos * freq;
            float fcr = cosf(val);
            float fci = sinf(val);
            int rotn = i < kv_dim ? 2 : 1; // how many vectors? 2 = q & k, 1 = q only
            for (int v = 0; v < rotn; v++) {
                float* vec = v == 0 ? s->q : s->k; // the vector to rotate (query or key)
                float v0 = vec[i];
                float v1 = vec[i+1];
                vec[i]   = v0 * fcr - v1 * fci;
                vec[i+1] = v0 * fci + v1 * fcr;
            }
        }

        // multihead attention. iterate over all heads
        int h;
        #pragma omp parallel for private(h)
        for (h = 0; h < p->n_heads; h++) {
            // get the query vector for this head
            float* q = s->q + h * head_size;
            // attention scores for this head
            float* att = s->att + h * p->seq_len;
            // iterate over all timesteps, including the current one
            for (int t = 0; t <= pos; t++) {
                // get the key vector for this head and at this timestep
                float* k = s->key_cache + loff + t * kv_dim + (h / kv_mul) * head_size;
                // calculate the attention score as the dot product of q and k
                float score = 0.0f;
                for (int i = 0; i < head_size; i++) {
                    score += q[i] * k[i];
                }
                score /= sqrtf(head_size);
                // save the score to the attention buffer
                att[t] = score;
            }

            // softmax the scores to get attention weights, from 0..pos inclusively
            softmax(att, pos + 1);

            // weighted sum of the values, store back into xb
            float* xb = s->xb + h * head_size;
            memset(xb, 0, head_size * sizeof(float));
            for (int t = 0; t <= pos; t++) {
                // get the value vector for this head and at this timestep
                float* v = s->value_cache + loff + t * kv_dim + (h / kv_mul) * head_size;
                // get the attention weight for this timestep
                float a = att[t];
                // accumulate the weighted value into xb
                for (int i = 0; i < head_size; i++) {
                    xb[i] += a * v[i];
                }
            }
        }

        // final matmul to get the output of the attention
        matmul(s->xb2, s->xb, w->wo + l*dim*dim, dim, dim);

        // residual connection back into x
        for (int i = 0; i < dim; i++) {
            x[i] += s->xb2[i];
        }

        // ffn rmsnorm
        rmsnorm(s->xb, x, w->rms_ffn_weight + l*dim, dim);

        // Now for FFN in PyTorch we have: self.w2(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w3(x))
        // first calculate self.w1(x) and self.w3(x)
        matmul(s->hb, s->xb, w->w1 + l*dim*hidden_dim, dim, hidden_dim);
        matmul(s->hb2, s->xb, w->w3 + l*dim*hidden_dim, dim, hidden_dim);

        // SwiGLU non-linearity
        for (int i = 0; i < hidden_dim; i++) {
            float val = s->hb[i];
            // silu(x)=x*σ(x), where σ(x) is the logistic sigmoid
            val *= (1.0f / (1.0f + expf(-val)));
            // elementwise multiply with w3(x)
            val *= s->hb2[i];
            s->hb[i] = val;
        }

        // final matmul to get the output of the ffn
        matmul(s->xb, s->hb, w->w2 + l*dim*hidden_dim, hidden_dim, dim);

        // residual connection
        for (int i = 0; i < dim; i++) {
            x[i] += s->xb[i];
        }
    }

    // final rmsnorm
    rmsnorm(x, x, w->rms_final_weight, dim);

    // classifier into logits
    matmul(s->logits, x, w->wcls, p->dim, p->vocab_size);
    return s->logits;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) Tokenizer that translates strings <-> tokens

typedef struct {
    char *str;
    int id;
} TokenIndex;

typedef struct {
    char** vocab;
    float* vocab_scores;
    TokenIndex *sorted_vocab;
    int vocab_size;
    unsigned int max_token_length;
    unsigned char byte_pieces[512]; // stores all single-byte strings
} Tokenizer;

int compare_tokens(const void *a, const void *b) {
    return strcmp(((TokenIndex*)a)->str, ((TokenIndex*)b)->str);
}

void build_tokenizer(Tokenizer* t, char* tokenizer_path, int vocab_size) {
    // i should have written the vocab_size into the tokenizer file... sigh
    t->vocab_size = vocab_size;
    // malloc space to hold the scores and the strings
    t->vocab = (char**)malloc(vocab_size * sizeof(char*));
    t->vocab_scores = (float*)malloc(vocab_size * sizeof(float));
    t->sorted_vocab = NULL; // initialized lazily
    for (int i = 0; i < 256; i++) {
        t->byte_pieces[i * 2] = (unsigned char)i;
        t->byte_pieces[i * 2 + 1] = '\0';
    }
    // read in the file
    FILE *file = fopen(tokenizer_path, "rb");
    if (!file) { fprintf(stderr, "couldn't load %s\n", tokenizer_path); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); }
    if (fread(&t->max_token_length, sizeof(int), 1, file) != 1) { fprintf(stderr, "failed read\n"); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); }
    int len;
    for (int i = 0; i < vocab_size; i++) {
        if (fread(t->vocab_scores + i, sizeof(float), 1, file) != 1) { fprintf(stderr, "failed read\n"); exit(EXIT_FAILURE);}
        if (fread(&len, sizeof(int), 1, file) != 1) { fprintf(stderr, "failed read\n"); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); }
        t->vocab[i] = (char *)malloc(len + 1);
        if (fread(t->vocab[i], len, 1, file) != 1) { fprintf(stderr, "failed read\n"); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); }
        t->vocab[i][len] = '\0'; // add the string terminating token
    }
    fclose(file);
}

void free_tokenizer(Tokenizer* t) {
    for (int i = 0; i < t->vocab_size; i++) { free(t->vocab[i]); }
    free(t->vocab);
    free(t->vocab_scores);
    free(t->sorted_vocab);
}

char* decode(Tokenizer* t, int prev_token, int token) {
    char *piece = t->vocab[token];
    // following BOS (1) token, sentencepiece decoder strips any leading whitespace (see PR #89)
    if (prev_token == 1 && piece[0] == ' ') { piece++; }
    // careful, some tokens designate raw bytes, and look like e.g. '<0x01>'
    // parse this and convert and return the actual byte
    unsigned char byte_val;
    if (sscanf(piece, "<0x%02hhX>", &byte_val) == 1) {
        piece = (char*)t->byte_pieces + byte_val * 2;
    }
    return piece;
}

void safe_printf(char *piece) {
    // piece might be a raw byte token, and we only want to print printable chars or whitespace
    // because some of the other bytes can be various control codes, backspace, etc.
    if (piece == NULL) { return; }
    if (piece[0] == '\0') { return; }
    if (piece[1] == '\0') {
        unsigned char byte_val = piece[0];
        if (!(isprint(byte_val) || isspace(byte_val))) {
            return; // bad byte, don't print it
        }
    }
    printf("%s", piece);
}

int str_lookup(char *str, TokenIndex *sorted_vocab, int vocab_size) {
    // efficiently find the perfect match for str in vocab, return its index or -1 if not found
    TokenIndex tok = { .str = str }; // acts as the key to search for
    TokenIndex *res = bsearch(&tok, sorted_vocab, vocab_size, sizeof(TokenIndex), compare_tokens);
    return res != NULL ? res->id : -1;
}

void encode(Tokenizer* t, char *text, int8_t bos, int8_t eos, int *tokens, int *n_tokens) {
    // encode the string text (input) into an upper-bound preallocated tokens[] array
    // bos != 0 means prepend the BOS token (=1), eos != 0 means append the EOS token (=2)
    if (text == NULL) { fprintf(stderr, "cannot encode NULL text\n"); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); }

    if (t->sorted_vocab == NULL) {
        // lazily malloc and sort the vocabulary
        t->sorted_vocab = malloc(t->vocab_size * sizeof(TokenIndex));
        for (int i = 0; i < t->vocab_size; i++) {
            t->sorted_vocab[i].str = t->vocab[i];
            t->sorted_vocab[i].id = i;
        }
        qsort(t->sorted_vocab, t->vocab_size, sizeof(TokenIndex), compare_tokens);
    }

    // create a temporary buffer that will store merge candidates of always two consecutive tokens
    // *2 for concat, +1 for null terminator +2 for UTF8 (in case max_token_length is 1)
    char* str_buffer = malloc((t->max_token_length*2 +1 +2) * sizeof(char));
    size_t str_len = 0;

    // start at 0 tokens
    *n_tokens = 0;

    // add optional BOS (=1) token, if desired
    if (bos) tokens[(*n_tokens)++] = 1;

    // add_dummy_prefix is true by default
    // so prepend a dummy prefix token to the input string, but only if text != ""
    // TODO: pretty sure this isn't correct in the general case but I don't have the
    // energy to read more of the sentencepiece code to figure out what it's doing
    if (text[0] != '\0') {
        int dummy_prefix = str_lookup(" ", t->sorted_vocab, t->vocab_size);
        tokens[(*n_tokens)++] = dummy_prefix;
    }

    // Okay UTF-8 time. This will get messy. Here is the reference from Wikipedia:
    // Code point ↔ UTF-8 conversion
    // First code point	Last code point	Byte 1	Byte 2	Byte 3	Byte 4
    // U+0000	U+007F	    0xxxxxxx
    // U+0080	U+07FF	    110xxxxx	10xxxxxx
    // U+0800	U+FFFF	    1110xxxx	10xxxxxx	10xxxxxx
    // U+10000	U+10FFFF    11110xxx	10xxxxxx	10xxxxxx	10xxxxxx

    // process the raw (UTF-8) byte sequence of the input string
    for (char *c = text; *c != '\0'; c++) {

        // reset buffer if the current byte is ASCII or a leading byte
        // 0xC0 is 11000000, so (*c & 0xC0) keeps the first 2 bits and zeros the rest
        // 0x80 is 10000000
        // in UTF-8, all continuation bytes start with "10" in first two bits
        // so in English this is: "if this byte is not a continuation byte"
        if ((*c & 0xC0) != 0x80) {
            // this byte must be either a leading byte (11...) or an ASCII char (0x...)
            // => reset our location, as we're starting a new UTF-8 codepoint
            str_len = 0;
        }

        // append the current byte to the buffer
        str_buffer[str_len++] = *c; // ++ is post-increment, incremented after this line
        str_buffer[str_len] = '\0';

        // while the next character is a continuation byte, continue appending
        // but if there are too many of them, just stop to avoid overruning str_buffer size.
        if ((*(c+1) & 0xC0) == 0x80 && str_len < 4) {
            continue;
        }

        // ok c+1 is not a continuation byte, so we've read in a full codepoint
        int id = str_lookup(str_buffer, t->sorted_vocab, t->vocab_size);

        if (id != -1) {
            // we found this codepoint in vocab, add it as a token
            tokens[(*n_tokens)++] = id;
        } else {
            // byte_fallback encoding: just encode each byte as a token
            // +3 is here because the first 3 vocab elements are <unk>, <s>, </s>
            // so the individual bytes only start at index 3
            for (int i=0; i < str_len; i++) {
                tokens[(*n_tokens)++] = (unsigned char)str_buffer[i] + 3;
            }
        }
        str_len = 0; // protect against a sequence of stray UTF8 continuation bytes
    }

    // merge the best consecutive pair each iteration, according the scores in vocab_scores
    while (1) {
        float best_score = -1e10;
        int best_id = -1;
        int best_idx = -1;

        for (int i=0; i < (*n_tokens-1); i++) {
            // check if we can merge the pair (tokens[i], tokens[i+1])
            sprintf(str_buffer, "%s%s", t->vocab[tokens[i]], t->vocab[tokens[i+1]]);
            int id = str_lookup(str_buffer, t->sorted_vocab, t->vocab_size);
            if (id != -1 && t->vocab_scores[id] > best_score) {
                // this merge pair exists in vocab! record its score and position
                best_score = t->vocab_scores[id];
                best_id = id;
                best_idx = i;
            }
        }

        if (best_idx == -1) {
            break; // we couldn't find any more pairs to merge, so we're done
        }

        // merge the consecutive pair (best_idx, best_idx+1) into new token best_id
        tokens[best_idx] = best_id;
        // delete token at position best_idx+1, shift the entire sequence back 1
        for (int i = best_idx+1; i < (*n_tokens-1); i++) {
            tokens[i] = tokens[i+1];
        }
        (*n_tokens)--; // token length decreased
    }

    // add optional EOS (=2) token, if desired
    if (eos) tokens[(*n_tokens)++] = 2;

    free(str_buffer);
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The Sampler, which takes logits and returns a sampled token
// sampling can be done in a few ways: greedy argmax, sampling, top-p sampling

typedef struct {
    float prob;
    int index;
} ProbIndex; // struct used when sorting probabilities during top-p sampling

typedef struct {
    int vocab_size;
    ProbIndex* probindex; // buffer used in top-p sampling
    float temperature;
    float topp;
    unsigned long long rng_state;
} Sampler;

int sample_argmax(float* probabilities, int n) {
    // return the index that has the highest probability
    int max_i = 0;
    float max_p = probabilities[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (probabilities[i] > max_p) {
            max_i = i;
            max_p = probabilities[i];
        }
    }
    return max_i;
}

int sample_mult(float* probabilities, int n, float coin) {
    // sample index from probabilities (they must sum to 1!)
    // coin is a random number in [0, 1), usually from random_f32()
    float cdf = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        cdf += probabilities[i];
        if (coin < cdf) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return n - 1; // in case of rounding errors
}

int compare(const void* a, const void* b) {
    ProbIndex* a_ = (ProbIndex*) a;
    ProbIndex* b_ = (ProbIndex*) b;
    if (a_->prob > b_->prob) return -1;
    if (a_->prob < b_->prob) return 1;
    return 0;
}

int sample_topp(float* probabilities, int n, float topp, ProbIndex* probindex, float coin) {
    // top-p sampling (or "nucleus sampling") samples from the smallest set of
    // tokens that exceed probability topp. This way we never sample tokens that
    // have very low probabilities and are less likely to go "off the rails".
    // coin is a random number in [0, 1), usually from random_f32()

    int n0 = 0;
    // quicksort indices in descending order of probabilities
    // values smaller than (1 - topp) / (n - 1) cannot be part of the result
    // so for efficiency we crop these out as candidates before sorting
    const float cutoff = (1.0f - topp) / (n - 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (probabilities[i] >= cutoff) {
            probindex[n0].index = i;
            probindex[n0].prob = probabilities[i];
            n0++;
        }
    }
    qsort(probindex, n0, sizeof(ProbIndex), compare);

    // truncate the list where cumulative probability exceeds topp
    float cumulative_prob = 0.0f;
    int last_idx = n0 - 1; // in case of rounding errors consider all elements
    for (int i = 0; i < n0; i++) {
        cumulative_prob += probindex[i].prob;
        if (cumulative_prob > topp) {
            last_idx = i;
            break; // we've exceeded topp by including last_idx
        }
    }

    // sample from the truncated list
    float r = coin * cumulative_prob;
    float cdf = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i <= last_idx; i++) {
        cdf += probindex[i].prob;
        if (r < cdf) {
            return probindex[i].index;
        }
    }
    return probindex[last_idx].index; // in case of rounding errors
}

void build_sampler(Sampler* sampler, int vocab_size, float temperature, float topp, unsigned long long rng_seed) {
    sampler->vocab_size = vocab_size;
    sampler->temperature = temperature;
    sampler->topp = topp;
    sampler->rng_state = rng_seed;
    // buffer only used with nucleus sampling; may not need but it's ~small
    sampler->probindex = malloc(sampler->vocab_size * sizeof(ProbIndex));
}

void free_sampler(Sampler* sampler) {
    free(sampler->probindex);
}

unsigned int random_u32(unsigned long long *state) {
    // xorshift rng: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xorshift#xorshift.2A
    *state ^= *state >> 12;
    *state ^= *state << 25;
    *state ^= *state >> 27;
    return (*state * 0x2545F4914F6CDD1Dull) >> 32;
}
float random_f32(unsigned long long *state) { // random float32 in [0,1)
    return (random_u32(state) >> 8) / 16777216.0f;
}

int sample(Sampler* sampler, float* logits) {
    // sample the token given the logits and some hyperparameters
    int next;
    if (sampler->temperature == 0.0f) {
        // greedy argmax sampling: take the token with the highest probability
        next = sample_argmax(logits, sampler->vocab_size);
    } else {
        // apply the temperature to the logits
        for (int q=0; q<sampler->vocab_size; q++) { logits[q] /= sampler->temperature; }
        // apply softmax to the logits to get the probabilities for next token
        softmax(logits, sampler->vocab_size);
        // flip a (float) coin (this is our source of entropy for sampling)
        float coin = random_f32(&sampler->rng_state);
        // we sample from this distribution to get the next token
        if (sampler->topp <= 0 || sampler->topp >= 1) {
            // simply sample from the predicted probability distribution
            next = sample_mult(logits, sampler->vocab_size, coin);
        } else {
            // top-p (nucleus) sampling, clamping the least likely tokens to zero
            next = sample_topp(logits, sampler->vocab_size, sampler->topp, sampler->probindex, coin);
        }
    }
    return next;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// utilities: time

long time_in_ms() {
    // return time in milliseconds, for benchmarking the model speed
    struct timespec time;
    clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME, &time);
    return time.tv_sec * 1000 + time.tv_nsec / 1000000;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// generation loop

void generate(Transformer *transformer, Tokenizer *tokenizer, Sampler *sampler, char *prompt, int steps) {
    char *empty_prompt = "";
    if (prompt == NULL) { prompt = empty_prompt; }

    // encode the (string) prompt into tokens sequence
    int num_prompt_tokens = 0;
    int* prompt_tokens = (int*)malloc((strlen(prompt)+3) * sizeof(int)); // +3 for '\0', ?BOS, ?EOS
    encode(tokenizer, prompt, 1, 0, prompt_tokens, &num_prompt_tokens);
    if (num_prompt_tokens < 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "something is wrong, expected at least 1 prompt token\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // start the main loop
    long start = 0;  // used to time our code, only initialized after first iteration
    int next;        // will store the next token in the sequence
    int token = prompt_tokens[0]; // kick off with the first token in the prompt
    int pos = 0;     // position in the sequence
    while (pos < steps) {

        // forward the transformer to get logits for the next token
        float* logits = forward(transformer, token, pos);

        // advance the state machine
        if (pos < num_prompt_tokens - 1) {
            // if we are still processing the input prompt, force the next prompt token
            next = prompt_tokens[pos + 1];
        } else {
            // otherwise sample the next token from the logits
            next = sample(sampler, logits);
        }
        pos++;

        // data-dependent terminating condition: the BOS (=1) token delimits sequences
        if (next == 1) { break; }

        // print the token as string, decode it with the Tokenizer object
        char* piece = decode(tokenizer, token, next);
        safe_printf(piece); // same as printf("%s", piece), but skips "unsafe" bytes
        fflush(stdout);
        token = next;

        // init the timer here because the first iteration can be slower
        if (start == 0) { start = time_in_ms(); }
    }
    printf("\n");

    // report achieved tok/s (pos-1 because the timer starts after first iteration)
    if (pos > 1) {
        long end = time_in_ms();
        fprintf(stderr, "achieved tok/s: %f\n", (pos-1) / (double)(end-start)*1000);
    }

    free(prompt_tokens);
}

void read_stdin(const char* guide, char* buffer, size_t bufsize) {
    // read a line from stdin, up to but not including \n
    printf("%s", guide);
    if (fgets(buffer, bufsize, stdin) != NULL) {
        size_t len = strlen(buffer);
        if (len > 0 && buffer[len - 1] == '\n') {
            buffer[len - 1] = '\0'; // strip newline
        }
    }
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// chat loop
// I manually inspected the tokens for a few chat conversations compared to
// python reference and that seemed ok, but this was not thoroughly tested and
// is not safely implemented, it's more a proof of concept atm.

void chat(Transformer *transformer, Tokenizer *tokenizer, Sampler *sampler,
          char *cli_user_prompt, char *cli_system_prompt, int steps) {

    // buffers for reading the system prompt and user prompt from stdin
    // you'll notice they are soomewhat haphazardly and unsafely set atm
    char system_prompt[512];
    char user_prompt[512];
    char rendered_prompt[1152];
    int num_prompt_tokens = 0;
    int* prompt_tokens = (int*)malloc(1152 * sizeof(int));
    int user_idx;

    // start the main loop
    int8_t user_turn = 1; // user starts
    int next;        // will store the next token in the sequence
    int token;       // stores the current token to feed into the transformer
    int prev_token;
    int pos = 0;     // position in the sequence
    while (pos < steps) {

        // when it is the user's turn to contribute tokens to the dialog...
        if (user_turn) {
            // get the (optional) system prompt at position 0
            if (pos == 0) {
                // at position 0, the user can also contribute a system prompt
                if (cli_system_prompt == NULL) {
                    // system prompt was not passed in, attempt to get it from stdin
                    read_stdin("Enter system prompt (optional): ", system_prompt, sizeof(system_prompt));
                } else {
                    // system prompt was passed in, use it
                    strcpy(system_prompt, cli_system_prompt);
                }
            }
            // get the user prompt
            if (pos == 0 && cli_user_prompt != NULL) {
                // user prompt for position 0 was passed in, use it
                strcpy(user_prompt, cli_user_prompt);
            } else {
                // otherwise get user prompt from stdin
                read_stdin("User: ", user_prompt, sizeof(user_prompt));
            }
            // render user/system prompts into the Llama 2 Chat schema
            if (pos == 0 && system_prompt[0] != '\0') {
                char system_template[] = "[INST] <<SYS>>\n%s\n<</SYS>>\n\n%s [/INST]";
                sprintf(rendered_prompt, system_template, system_prompt, user_prompt);
            } else {
                char user_template[] = "[INST] %s [/INST]";
                sprintf(rendered_prompt, user_template, user_prompt);
            }
            // encode the rendered prompt into tokens
            encode(tokenizer, rendered_prompt, 1, 0, prompt_tokens, &num_prompt_tokens);
            user_idx = 0; // reset the user index
            user_turn = 0;
            printf("Assistant: ");
        }

        // determine the token to pass into the transformer next
        if (user_idx < num_prompt_tokens) {
            // if we are still processing the input prompt, force the next prompt token
            token = prompt_tokens[user_idx++];
        } else {
            // otherwise use the next token sampled from previous turn
            token = next;
        }
        // EOS (=2) token ends the Assistant turn
        if (token == 2) { user_turn = 1; }

        // forward the transformer to get logits for the next token
        float* logits = forward(transformer, token, pos);
        next = sample(sampler, logits);
        pos++;

        if (user_idx >= num_prompt_tokens && next != 2) {
            // the Assistant is responding, so print its output
            char* piece = decode(tokenizer, token, next);
            safe_printf(piece); // same as printf("%s", piece), but skips "unsafe" bytes
            fflush(stdout);
        }
        if (next == 2) { printf("\n"); }
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(prompt_tokens);
}

void error_usage() {
    fprintf(stderr, "Usage:   run <checkpoint> [options]\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "Example: run model.bin -n 256 -i \"Once upon a time\"\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "Options:\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -t <float>  temperature in [0,inf], default 1.0\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -p <float>  p value in top-p (nucleus) sampling in [0,1] default 0.9\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -s <int>    random seed, default time(NULL)\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -n <int>    number of steps to run for, default 256. 0 = max_seq_len\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -i <string> input prompt\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -z <string> optional path to custom tokenizer\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -m <string> mode: generate|chat, default: generate\n");
    fprintf(stderr, "  -y <string> (optional) system prompt in chat mode\n");
    exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {

    // default parameters
    char *checkpoint_path = NULL;  // e.g. out/model.bin
    char *tokenizer_path = "tokenizer.bin";
    float temperature = 1.0f;   // 0.0 = greedy deterministic. 1.0 = original. don't set higher
    float topp = 0.9f;          // top-p in nucleus sampling. 1.0 = off. 0.9 works well, but slower
    int steps = 256;            // number of steps to run for
    char *prompt = NULL;        // prompt string
    unsigned long long rng_seed = 0; // seed rng with time by default
    char *mode = "generate";    // generate|chat
    char *system_prompt = NULL; // the (optional) system prompt to use in chat mode

    // poor man's C argparse so we can override the defaults above from the command line
    if (argc >= 2) { checkpoint_path = argv[1]; } else { error_usage(); }
    for (int i = 2; i < argc; i+=2) {
        // do some basic validation
        if (i + 1 >= argc) { error_usage(); } // must have arg after flag
        if (argv[i][0] != '-') { error_usage(); } // must start with dash
        if (strlen(argv[i]) != 2) { error_usage(); } // must be -x (one dash, one letter)
        // read in the args
        if (argv[i][1] == 't') { temperature = atof(argv[i + 1]); }
        else if (argv[i][1] == 'p') { topp = atof(argv[i + 1]); }
        else if (argv[i][1] == 's') { rng_seed = atoi(argv[i + 1]); }
        else if (argv[i][1] == 'n') { steps = atoi(argv[i + 1]); }
        else if (argv[i][1] == 'i') { prompt = argv[i + 1]; }
        else if (argv[i][1] == 'z') { tokenizer_path = argv[i + 1]; }
        else if (argv[i][1] == 'm') { mode = argv[i + 1]; }
        else if (argv[i][1] == 'y') { system_prompt = argv[i + 1]; }
        else { error_usage(); }
    }

    // parameter validation/overrides
    if (rng_seed <= 0) rng_seed = (unsigned int)time(NULL);
    if (temperature < 0.0) temperature = 0.0;
    if (topp < 0.0 || 1.0 < topp) topp = 0.9;
    if (steps < 0) steps = 0;

    // build the Transformer via the model .bin file
    Transformer transformer;
    build_transformer(&transformer, checkpoint_path);
    if (steps == 0 || steps > transformer.config.seq_len) steps = transformer.config.seq_len; // override to ~max length

    // build the Tokenizer via the tokenizer .bin file
    Tokenizer tokenizer;
    build_tokenizer(&tokenizer, tokenizer_path, transformer.config.vocab_size);

    // build the Sampler
    Sampler sampler;
    build_sampler(&sampler, transformer.config.vocab_size, temperature, topp, rng_seed);

    // run!
    if (strcmp(mode, "generate") == 0) {
        generate(&transformer, &tokenizer, &sampler, prompt, steps);
    } else if (strcmp(mode, "chat") == 0) {
        chat(&transformer, &tokenizer, &sampler, prompt, system_prompt, steps);
    } else {
        fprintf(stderr, "unknown mode: %s\n", mode);
        error_usage();
    }

    // memory and file handles cleanup
    free_sampler(&sampler);
    free_tokenizer(&tokenizer);
    free_transformer(&transformer);
    return 0;
}

werk layout grammar — llama2c-checkpoint/1
==========================================

The binary layout of the file this package carries as `model/stories15M.bin`.

This grammar exists because of law 2: a werk package must carry the knowledge
needed to read its own bytes, and "it is a llama2.c checkpoint" is a name, not
a grammar. Everything below is DERIVED FROM THE RUNTIME SOURCE this package
also carries (`tools/llama2c/run.c`, functions `read_checkpoint` and
`memory_map_weights`) and then CHECKED against the actual file: the offsets in
§4 were computed from the header in §2 and they account for every one of the
file's 60 816 028 bytes with nothing left over. That check is the only reason
this document is allowed to say "MUST" anywhere.

Unlike the layouts in `spec/layouts/`, this is NOT a werk envelope. There is no
`WK**` magic, no MessagePack header and no section table. It is a foreign
format — a bare header followed by bare tensors — and werk's job here is to
describe it exactly rather than to convert it. That is the honest thing for a
container to do with a third-party artifact whose bytes must stay byte-identical
to what its author published.

1. SCALARS AND ENDIANNESS
-------------------------

  i32  signed 32-bit integer, two's complement, LITTLE-ENDIAN
  f32  IEEE 754 binary32, LITTLE-ENDIAN

The file declares no endianness of its own. Little-endian is what the runtime
assumes (it `mmap`s the bytes and casts) and it is what the manifest's
`conventions.endianness = "le"` declares for this package. A big-endian consumer
MUST byte-swap and MUST NOT read the file in place.

There is no magic number, no version field and no checksum anywhere in this
format. A reader therefore cannot tell a truncated or wrong file from a valid
one by inspection; it can only check the arithmetic of §4 against the file size.
This grammar makes that check normative:

  MUST: a conformant reader computes the total from §4 and REFUSES the file
  (node-scoped refusal, SPEC.md §10.1) when it does not equal the file size.

The manifest's own `sha256` for `model/stories15M.bin` is the stronger check and
is the one a werk reader has anyway.

2. HEADER — 28 bytes at offset 0
--------------------------------

Seven i32 in this order. These are the fields of `Config` in run.c, in
declaration order, read by one `fread(config, sizeof(Config), 1, file)`.

  off  type  name          value in model/stories15M.bin
  ---  ----  ------------  -----------------------------
    0  i32   dim                288
    4  i32   hidden_dim         768
    8  i32   n_layers             6
   12  i32   n_heads              6
   16  i32   n_kv_heads           6
   20  i32   vocab_size       32000
   24  i32   seq_len            256

Derived quantities used by §4:

  head_size = dim / n_heads                 = 48
  kv_dim    = (dim * n_kv_heads) / n_heads  = 288

THE SIGN OF `vocab_size` IS A FLAG. run.c:

    int shared_weights = config->vocab_size > 0 ? 1 : 0;
    config->vocab_size = abs(config->vocab_size);

A POSITIVE `vocab_size` means the output classifier SHARES the token embedding
table; a NEGATIVE one means a separate classifier matrix follows the RoPE
tables. In this file the value is +32000, so the weights ARE shared and there is
no trailing classifier. run.c's own comment on this is "bit yikes." It is
recorded here rather than smoothed over, because a reader that misses it reads
either 36 864 000 bytes too few or too many.

3. TENSOR ELEMENT TYPE
----------------------

Every tensor in this file is f32. There is no quantisation, no scale, no
zero-point and no per-block metadata anywhere in this format. (llama2.c has a
separate int8 checkpoint format, `version 2`, written by a different exporter
with an explicit magic and version header; this file is NOT that and a reader
must not look for one.)

Tensors are stored DENSE, ROW-MAJOR, C order, with no padding and no alignment
between them. A tensor of shape (a, b, c) occupies a*b*c*4 bytes and element
(i, j, k) is at element index ((i*b) + j)*c + k.

4. TENSOR ORDER AND OFFSETS
---------------------------

Immediately after the 28-byte header, in exactly this order. Order is
load-bearing: nothing in the file names a tensor, so a tensor is identified only
by its position in this sequence. The order is `memory_map_weights` in run.c,
line for line.

  #   name                    shape             elements     offset      bytes
  --  ----------------------  ----------------  ---------  ----------  ---------
   1  token_embedding_table   (32000, 288)       9216000          28   36864000
   2  rms_att_weight          (6, 288)              1728    36864028       6912
   3  wq                      (6, 288, 288)       497664    36870940    1990656
   4  wk                      (6, 288, 288)       497664    38861596    1990656
   5  wv                      (6, 288, 288)       497664    40852252    1990656
   6  wo                      (6, 288, 288)       497664    42842908    1990656
   7  rms_ffn_weight          (6, 288)              1728    44833564       6912
   8  w1                      (6, 768, 288)      1327104    44840476    5308416
   9  w2                      (6, 288, 768)      1327104    50148892    5308416
  10  w3                      (6, 768, 288)      1327104    55457308    5308416
  11  rms_final_weight        (288,)                 288    60765724       1152
  12  (dead) freq_cis_real    (256, 24)             6144    60766876      24576
  13  (dead) freq_cis_imag    (256, 24)             6144    60791452      24576
  --  ----------------------  ----------------  ---------  ----------  ---------
                                                     total offset 60816028

  file size of model/stories15M.bin = 60 816 028 bytes.  EXACT MATCH, no slack.

The general shapes, for a checkpoint with other hyperparameters:

   1  token_embedding_table   (vocab_size, dim)
   2  rms_att_weight          (n_layers, dim)
   3  wq                      (n_layers, dim, n_heads * head_size)
   4  wk                      (n_layers, dim, n_kv_heads * head_size)
   5  wv                      (n_layers, dim, n_kv_heads * head_size)
   6  wo                      (n_layers, n_heads * head_size, dim)
   7  rms_ffn_weight          (n_layers, dim)
   8  w1                      (n_layers, hidden_dim, dim)
   9  w2                      (n_layers, dim, hidden_dim)
  10  w3                      (n_layers, hidden_dim, dim)
  11  rms_final_weight        (dim,)
  12  (dead) freq_cis_real    (seq_len, head_size / 2)
  13  (dead) freq_cis_imag    (seq_len, head_size / 2)
  14  wcls                    (vocab_size, dim)   — ONLY when vocab_size < 0

ENTRIES 12 AND 13 ARE DEAD SPACE AND MUST STILL BE SKIPPED. run.c says so in
two comments — "skip what used to be freq_cis_real (for RoPE)" — and reads
nothing from them: RoPE frequencies are recomputed on the fly in `forward()`.
They are 49 152 bytes of a format that keeps them only so old checkpoints stay
readable. A reader that does not skip them lands 49 152 bytes early on entry 14
and, in a shared-weights file like this one, silently reads the wrong end of the
file when it looks for anything after `rms_final_weight`.

5. WHAT THIS GRAMMAR DOES NOT TELL YOU
--------------------------------------

It tells you where every number is. It does not tell you what the numbers MEAN
as an architecture: the residual stream, the RMSNorm epsilon (1e-5f), the RoPE
base (10000.0f), the SwiGLU in the FFN, the softmax and the sampler all live in
`tools/llama2c/run.c`, which this package carries as source for exactly that
reason. This document and that file are the two halves of "you can read these
bytes"; neither is sufficient alone, and the split is deliberate — a layout
grammar that also tried to be a model definition would be a paper, not a
grammar.

6. DECISIONS
------------

D-L2C-1  No conversion. The checkpoint travels byte-identical to what its
         author published (sha256 in the manifest), because a package whose
         payload does not hash to the upstream artifact cannot be checked
         against upstream at all. Re-serialising it into a werk envelope would
         have bought a section table and cost the one property that makes the
         provenance verifiable by a stranger.

D-L2C-2  The dead RoPE tables are documented as dead rather than deleted, for
         the same reason: deleting them would change the bytes.

D-L2C-3  The offsets in §4 are stated absolutely, not as a formula the reader
         must evaluate. Law 8's corollary: never make a reader derive an offset
         it could have been told. The formula is given too, in §4's second
         table, for checkpoints that are not this one.



===== spec/layouts/llama2c-tokenizer.layout.txt (complete) =====
werk layout grammar — llama2c-tokenizer/1
=========================================

The binary layout of the file this package carries as `model/tokenizer.bin`.
Derived from `build_tokenizer`, `encode` and `decode` in `tools/llama2c/run.c`,
and checked against the file: the walk in §3 consumes exactly 433 869 bytes and
yields exactly 32 000 entries, with nothing left over.

1. SCALARS
----------

  i32  signed 32-bit integer, LITTLE-ENDIAN
  f32  IEEE 754 binary32, LITTLE-ENDIAN
  u8   raw byte

No magic number, no version, no checksum, and — the important omission — NO
VOCABULARY SIZE. See §4.

2. HEADER — 4 bytes at offset 0
-------------------------------

  off  type  name               value in model/tokenizer.bin
  ---  ----  -----------------  ----------------------------
    0  i32   max_token_length             27

`max_token_length` is the length in bytes of the longest token string in the
file. It is a buffer hint for the encoder, not a structural field. MEASURED over
this file: the longest entry is 27 bytes, so the declared value is correct. A
reader SHOULD check it rather than trust it; a wrong value here overflows a
fixed buffer in a naive encoder and nothing else in the file contradicts it.

3. ENTRIES — 32 000 records, packed, starting at offset 4
---------------------------------------------------------

Each record, with no padding between records and none at the end:

  type       name    meaning
  ---------  ------  --------------------------------------------------------
  f32        score   the BPE merge score. Higher wins. See §5.
  i32        len     length of `bytes` in bytes. NOT null-terminated in file.
  u8[len]    bytes   the token's UTF-8 text, verbatim

The token's ID is its ORDINAL POSITION in this sequence, counting from 0. The
file never writes an id down. This is the same property the checkpoint's tensor
order has and it has the same consequence: order is load-bearing and a reader
that skips a malformed record silently renumbers every token after it.

  MUST: a conformant reader walks all `vocab_size` records and REFUSES the file
  (node-scoped refusal, SPEC.md §10.1) if the walk does not land exactly on the
  end of the file. For this file that landing point is byte 433 869.

The first eight entries of model/tokenizer.bin, as a test vector for the walk:

  id  score  len  bytes
  --  -----  ---  --------------
   0    0.0    5  "<unk>"
   1    0.0    5  "\n<s>\n"
   2    0.0    6  "\n</s>\n"
   3    0.0    6  "<0x00>"
   4    0.0    6  "<0x01>"
   5    0.0    6  "<0x02>"
   6    0.0    6  "<0x03>"
   7    0.0    6  "<0x04>"

Ids 1 and 2 are BOS and EOS. Ids 3..258 are the 256 single-byte fallback
tokens, written as the six-character text "<0xNN>" — the text is the LITERAL
angle-bracket spelling, not the byte itself, and `decode` in run.c recognises
that spelling and substitutes the raw byte. A reader that emits "<0x0A>" where a
newline was meant has read the file correctly and decoded it wrongly.

4. THE MISSING FIELD, AND WHERE THE COUNT COMES FROM
----------------------------------------------------

THE NUMBER OF ENTRIES IS NOT IN THIS FILE. run.c carries the author's own note
about it:

    // i should have written the vocab_size into the tokenizer file... sigh

The count is passed in from the CHECKPOINT's header: `build_tokenizer` is called
with `transformer.config.vocab_size`. So `model/tokenizer.bin` cannot be read
without `model/stories15M.bin`, and the two files are only jointly meaningful.

That is a cross-file dependency inside one package, and werk states it rather
than leaving a reader to discover it:

  * the manifest's `x.model.tokenizer` node carries `meta.vocab_size = 32000`
    and `meta.vocab_size_source = "checkpoint header field 6"`, so a consumer
    holding only this node still knows the number;
  * `MUST`: where the two disagree, a reader reports the disagreement and does
    not pick one. The checkpoint's value is what the runtime will use, and a
    tokenizer walk that does not terminate on the file's last byte is the
    symptom.

A reader that has ONLY this file, and no checkpoint, can still recover the count
by walking to EOF and counting — which is what makes §3's "MUST land exactly on
the end" worth stating. It works for this file. It is not a general recovery:
any prefix of a valid record stream is also a valid record stream.

5. WHAT THE SCORES ARE FOR
--------------------------

`encode` in run.c is a greedy merging BPE: it first maps the input string to
single-byte and single-character tokens by exact lookup, then repeatedly finds
the adjacent pair whose CONCATENATION exists in the vocabulary with the highest
`score`, and merges it, until no pair merges. The scores are therefore a merge
PRIORITY, not a probability and not a log-likelihood, and nothing in the file or
the runtime normalises them.

Two details a re-implementation gets wrong and this package's test vectors
catch (`testvectors/vectors.json`):

  * a BOS token (id 1) is prepended by `generate()`;
  * SentencePiece encodes a leading space as U+2581, and run.c emulates that by
    prepending a "dummy prefix" space token to a non-empty prompt before
    merging. Drop it and the first generated token changes.

6. DECISIONS
------------

D-L2T-1  Carried byte-identical to upstream, for the reason D-L2C-1 gives.

D-L2T-2  `vocab_size` is duplicated into the node's `meta` rather than into the
         payload. Editing the payload to add the field the author wishes he had
         written would have broken the upstream hash — and law 9 says the
         manifest is where a consumer looks before opening a payload anyway.
